title: Sell Mineral Rights in Monroe County, AL
metaTitle: Sell Mineral Rights in Monroe County, AL | South AL Oil
metaDescription: Hold mineral or royalty interests in Monroe County, Alabama? Get a title-researched offer from a family-office buyer who reads the Monroeville records himself.
heroLead: Monroe County sits in the quieter stretch of Alabama's south-state oil country, between the Citronelle trend to the west and the Smackover tests that have worked their way through this part of the state for decades.
intro: Monroe County doesn't get talked about the way Mobile or Escambia County does, but families here have held mineral and royalty interests for generations, often tied to leasing activity that swept through south Alabama in waves — a round in the 1950s and 1960s chasing shallower production, and later rounds testing deeper Jurassic-age Smackover and Norphlet targets as operators pushed further to find what the Citronelle Field had already proven was possible nearby. Most of what we see in this county is older acreage, passed down through two or three generations, where the current owner has a vague sense that “there's oil and gas under there somewhere” but no clear picture of what's actually leased, what's producing, or what any of it is worth today.

We buy mineral and royalty interests directly, and in Monroe County that starts with the courthouse in Monroeville, the county seat. Before we quote anyone a number, we pull the conveyance and probate books ourselves to see what was actually conveyed, whether the mineral estate was ever severed from the surface, and how many heirs the interest has passed through since the original owner held it.

sections.heading: Scattered Leasing Waves Instead of One Big Field
paragraphs: Unlike Mobile County, which has one dominant field defining most of its production history, Monroe County's oil and gas story is more scattered — exploratory leasing that came and went as operators tested different formations at different depths. That pattern means ownership here is genuinely mixed: some tracts sit near wells with real production history, others were leased decades ago, tested, and never drilled, and a fair number were leased, held for a primary term, and simply released back to the mineral owner without anyone telling the family what that meant.

If your interest has never produced, that doesn't make it worthless, but it does mean the conversation about value has to start with the lease and title history rather than a royalty statement, because there may not be one.

sections.heading: Heirs' Property and Tenancy in Common
paragraphs: Monroe County has a lot of rural land that passed through families without formal wills, which is exactly how heirs' property situations develop — a mineral interest ends up owned by a shifting group of siblings, cousins, and in-laws as tenants in common, often without a clean paper trail connecting the current generation back to the original grantee. We see this constantly in this county specifically, and it's usually the single biggest thing slowing a sale down, more than the geology.

Untangling it starts with the probate file for whichever ancestor last held clear title, then working forward through each subsequent estate. It's tedious, but it's necessary, and we do that work ourselves rather than asking a family to hire a title attorney before we'll even talk.

sections.heading: Split Estate From Old Timber and Turpentine Land
paragraphs: A meaningful share of Monroe County's rural land moved through timber companies in the early and mid-twentieth century, some of it originally tied to the turpentine and naval stores industry that worked this part of Alabama before large-scale pulpwood took over. Those transactions frequently severed the mineral estate from the surface, which means plenty of families who own the surface today don't own what's under it, and the reverse is just as common — a family that sold the surface generations ago but kept the minerals, unaware that those minerals still have value independent of the land itself.

sections.heading: What We Look At Before Making an Offer
paragraphs: Value in Monroe County depends on proximity to whatever leasing or drilling activity has occurred nearby, whether the tract has ever been included in a producing unit, and — for interests that have produced — what recent royalty checks actually show. We price against that real, current information, not a flat per-acre number pulled from a neighboring parish or county, because activity in south Alabama varies block by block, not county by county.

faqs.question: My grandfather's lease from decades ago expired with no well drilled. Do we still own the minerals?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes — an expired lease with no production simply reverts the mineral rights to the owner, it doesn't transfer ownership. We'd confirm that against the courthouse record before making an offer.

faqs.question: There's no clear will connecting us to the original owner. Can you still buy our interest?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes, though it takes more title work up front. We trace the probate chain ourselves starting from the last record holder, and we'll tell you honestly if something needs to be cleared up first.

faqs.question: How is Monroe County different from the bigger oil counties nearby?
faqs.answer: There's no single dominant field here the way Citronelle defines Mobile County. Activity has come in scattered leasing waves, so value depends much more on the specific tract's history than on the county as a whole.

faqs.question: We sold the surface years ago but think we kept the minerals. How do we check?
faqs.answer: Send us the old deed if you have it, or just the legal description. We'll pull the Monroe County records and tell you plainly whether the mineral reservation was actually recorded and still holds.
